message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Dominated by the most abundant isotope, protium (¹H). |
| **Isotopes** | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) | Deuterium and tritium are stable/long‑lived; tritium is radioactive (half‑life ~12.3 y). |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest among all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Highest of all elements. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Negative, meaning energy is released when H gains an electron. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; hydrogen is a gas at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Liquid hydrogen exists only under high pressure or cryogenic conditions. |
| **Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ | Less dense than air; it rises. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas, 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard molar volume. |
| **Molecular weight (H₂)** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ | Diatomic hydrogen gas. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Strong covalent bond in H₂. |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | H₂ is a non‑polar molecule. |
| **Reactivity** | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids, and many organic compounds. | Forms covalent bonds with many elements; can act as a reducing agent. |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | Weak acid (pKa ≈ 35) | In aqueous solution, H⁺ is solvated; H₂O is the solvent. |
| **Oxidation states** | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as H⁻), 0 (as H₂) | Can exist in three common oxidation states. |
| **Spectral features** | Strong absorption in the UV (Lyman series) and visible (Balmer series) | Key in astrophysics for identifying hydrogen in stars. |
| **Phase behavior** | Exists as a gas at ambient conditions; liquid under cryogenic temperatures; solid below ~13.8 K (under pressure). | Solid hydrogen has multiple crystalline phases (I, II, III, IV) under high pressure. |
| **Thermal conductivity** | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 20 K) | High compared to many gases. |
| **Specific heat capacity (gas)** | 14.304 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ (at 300 K) | Relatively high for a monatomic gas. |
| **Electrical conductivity** | Very low in neutral form; becomes conductive when ionized (plasma). | Ionized hydrogen (protons) is a key component of plasma in stars. |
| **Magnetic properties** | Diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons) | Weakly repelled by magnetic fields. |
| **Isotopic effects** | Deuterium and tritium have slightly different physical properties (e.g., higher boiling/melting points). | Used in nuclear fusion research (DT fusion). |

### Quick Takeaways

- **Atomic simplicity**: One proton, one electron → the simplest atom.
- **High reactivity**: Forms hydrides, acids, and fuels; essential in organic chemistry.
- **Low density & low boiling point**: Makes it a lightweight, cryogenic gas.
- **Isotopic diversity**: Protium (stable), deuterium (stable), tritium (radioactive) – each with distinct nuclear properties.
- **Astrophysical importance**: Dominant element in the universe; spectral lines (Lyman, Balmer) are fundamental to astronomy.
- **Energy relevance**: Hydrogen fuel cells, potential fusion fuel (DT), and as a clean energy vector.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
